extracted.intended_audience: readers of Victorian fiction and writers studying literary style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards distilled from a Thackeray comic travel vignette: how to shape satire, characterization, dialogue, and authorial stance in Victorian humorous fiction. Emphasizes clarity of figurative language, character-focused narrative, and social/detail-based comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's worth measured by learned style
rubrics_metrics.description: “such a genius is paid for his work: with such neat logic, such a pure style, such a charming poetical turn of phrase, of course a critic gets money.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative observation (ironical) that critics are valued and remunerated for polished scholarship and ornate phrasing (e.g., Latinate expressions, elaborate metaphors such as 'sardonic divings after the pearl of truth, whose lustre is eclipsed in the display of the diseased oyster'). Implicitly signals that cultivated, scholarly diction and clever rhetorical turns are treated as markers of critical authority (and remuneration). Also includes satirical remarks about the social investment (education, penalties) that produce such mannered critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with figures and similes (clarity of imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: “you should be more careful in making your figures figures, and your similes like: for instance, when you talk of a book 'swelling the tide of exhilaration incident to the inauguration of the new year,' or of a book 'bearing the stamp of its origin in vacuity,' &c.,--or of a man diving sardonically; or of a pearl eclipsed in the display of a diseased oyster--there are some people who will not apprehend your meaning: some will doubt whether you had a meaning: some even will question your great powers, and say, 'Is this man to be a critic in a newspaper...?'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit stylistic injunction: avoid over-wrought, obscure, or excessively ornamental metaphors that obscure meaning. Examples given as anti-patterns (over-latinized, convoluted imagery). Warns that such obscurity may prompt readers to doubt intention or competence. In short: make figures and similes clear and intelligible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow popular demand (sales) to outweigh a lone critic
rubrics_metrics.description: “But if, in spite of Tibbs... if the little farce... is asked for, even up to Twelfth Night,--shall the publisher stop because Tibbs is dissatisfied? Whenever that capitalist calls to get his money back, he may see the letter from the respected publisher, informing the author that all the copies are sold, and that there are demands for a new edition. Up with the curtain, then!... and no money returned, except the Times 'gratuity!'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical publishing guideline (argued humorously): commercial success and reader demand should determine whether a piece continues in print or performance, not the grumblings of a single 'cheap' critic. Anti-pattern: allowing one scornful reviewer to cancel a successful popular entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on feelings and characters rather than events and places
rubrics_metrics.description: “This is a chronicle of feelings and characters, not of events and places, so much.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial program: prioritize interior life, character sketches, social manners, and emotional nuance over plot-driven actions or travelogue description. The surrounding passages—night watches, suppressed confessions, subtle pangs of feeling—illustrate using small moments and internal reflection to drive interest rather than grand events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social detail, mimicry, and comic smallness to characterize
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the passage: comic particulars (the cabman charging six times fare; labeled luggage marked 'K'; the Kicklebury party's footman; imitations of Captain Hicks's drawl—'the Whine'—and hoods called 'UGLIES') are deployed to reveal class, pretension, and personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique guideline: evoke characters and social types by concentrated, often comic, concrete details; employ dialect, mannerisms, and mimicry to render personalities vividly. Small domestic or travel details (luggage, parasols, shawls, a footman's stoop, awkward curtsies) function as economical signals of status and comic contrast. Anti-pattern: abstract generalizations about characters without such grounding particulars.
